The authentication middleware processes each incoming request through a series of
validation steps before forwarding it to the route handler. First, the middleware
extracts the JWT token from the Authorization header. If no token is present, it
returns a 401 Unauthorized response immediately.

Once the token is extracted, it is decoded using the RS256 algorithm with the
server's public key. The payload contains the user ID, role, and expiration
timestamp. If decoding fails due to an invalid signature or malformed token, the
middleware logs the attempt with the client IP and returns a 403 Forbidden response.

The session validation step checks whether the user's session is still active in
the Redis cache. Sessions expire after 24 hours of inactivity, but active sessions
are extended by 30 minutes on each request. This sliding window approach balances
security with user experience.

After successful authentication, the middleware injects the user context into the
request extensions. Downstream handlers can access this context using the
`extract_user()` helper function, which returns a Result containing the User struct
or an AuthError if the context is missing.

Rate limiting is applied per-user using a token bucket algorithm. Each authenticated
user is allowed 100 requests per minute for standard endpoints, and 10 requests per
minute for write operations. Rate limit headers (X-RateLimit-Remaining and
X-RateLimit-Reset) are included in every response.

Error handling follows a consistent pattern throughout the middleware chain. All
errors are converted to a standardized ErrorResponse struct containing a machine-
readable error code, a human-readable message, and an optional details field for
validation errors. The error response is always JSON-formatted regardless of the
Accept header.
